title: Scarcity, Incentives and Trade-offs
bigQuestion: When you cannot have everything, how do you decide what is worth giving up?

story.title: The Kitchen-Table Spreadsheet
story.kicker: Maya has one summer and two good plans, and her family puts both on a spreadsheet.
paragraphs: It is a Sunday night in May in Aurora, Illinois. Maya is 14. Her aunt runs a garden center, and she has offered Maya a summer job. The pay is $12 an hour, 20 hours a week, for 8 weeks. (These numbers are an example.) The same week, Maya's school sent a flyer for a summer math program. It meets on the same weekday afternoons.

Maya's mom opens her laptop at the kitchen table. "Let's put both plans side by side," she says. She makes two columns: Job and Summer School. Down the side she types the things that matter to the family: money, learning, time with friends, getting ready for high school, and cost.

Maya's brother does the math for the job. Twenty hours times $12 is $240 a week. Eight weeks of that is $1,920. The summer program costs $150 for books and a bus pass, as an example. "So school costs $150," he says. Maya's mom shakes her head. "School costs $150 plus the $1,920 you would not earn. That is $2,070."

Maya frowns. She wants the money for a used laptop. She also wants to start algebra strong in the fall. She cannot do both on the same afternoons. Every choice she makes will give something up. That is the problem every person, family, school and country faces. Economists call it scarcity, and this chapter is about how to think it through.
story.think: Maya's mom said summer school really costs $2,070, not $150. Do you agree? What else, besides money, might Maya give up with each choice?

lessons.title: Scarcity Starts Everything
lessons.mainIdea: Scarcity means our wants are bigger than the time, money and resources we have, so we must choose.
reading: Picture your school cafeteria at lunch. There are 300 students and 20 minutes. There are 150 slices of pizza. If every student wants a slice, 150 students will not get one. The pizza is scarce. *Scarcity* means people want more than there is.

Scarcity is not the same as being poor. A billionaire still has only 24 hours in a day. A rich country still has only so many doctors. Scarcity is about limits. Time, money, land, workers and machines are all limited. Wants have no clear limit. When you get one thing, you usually want something else.

Because of scarcity, every person must make choices. That is why *economics* exists. Economics is the study of how people choose to use limited resources to meet their wants. It asks what we make, how we make it and who gets it.

A common mistake is to think scarcity means a shortage. A shortage is a short-term problem, like a store running out of a toy in December. Scarcity never goes away. Even with a full store, you still cannot buy everything in it.

words.d: the basic problem that people's wants are greater than the limited resources available to meet them
the study of how people make choices about using limited resources to meet their wants

look.title: One Saturday, Many Wants
look.text: Jordan has one free Saturday and $30. Jordan wants to go to a movie ($12 in this example), buy a video game ($30), play in a soccer game from 10 to 2, and finish a science project that takes 4 hours.
look.prompt: List two things Jordan cannot do together. Is Jordan's problem about money, time, or both?

check.q: Which statement best describes scarcity?
choices: Wants are greater than the resources available
A store runs out of a toy for one week
Only poor people have to make choices
Prices are too high for most people
check.why: Scarcity is the lasting gap between unlimited wants and limited resources. It affects rich and poor alike.

check.q: A billionaire wants to visit 5 cities in one day but can only reach 2. What is the scarce resource?
check.why: She has plenty of money, but time is limited. Scarcity applies to everyone.

check.q: How is a shortage different from scarcity?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing
Scarcity only happens in poor countries
A shortage is short-term; scarcity never goes away
check.why: A shortage is a temporary lack of a good. Scarcity is permanent because wants always outrun resources.

lessons.title: The Four Factors of Production
lessons.mainIdea: Everything is made with land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship, and all four are scarce.
reading: Think about a pizza shop on a Chicago corner. To make one pizza, the shop needs flour, tomatoes, cheese and water. It needs a cook. It needs an oven and a mixer. It needs someone who had the idea and took the risk to open the shop. Economists sort these into four groups called the *factors of production*.

*Land* means all natural resources: soil, water, trees, oil, and the space the shop sits on. *Labor* is human work and skill, like the cook and the cashier. *Capital* means tools, machines and buildings made to produce other goods, like the oven. Careful: in economics, capital is not money. Money buys capital, but the oven is the capital.

The fourth factor is *entrepreneurship*. An entrepreneur is a person who combines the other three and takes the risk of starting a business. If the pizza shop fails, the entrepreneur loses. If it succeeds, the entrepreneur earns a profit.

Each factor is scarce. There is only so much farmland in Illinois. There are only so many trained cooks. Ovens cost money to build. So a society must choose how to use its factors. Farmland used for corn cannot also grow soybeans the same season.

words.d: the resources used to make goods and services: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship
all natural resources, such as soil, water, minerals and forests
the work and skills people put into producing goods and services
tools, machines and buildings made by people and used to produce other goods and services
the effort of a person who combines resources and takes the risk of starting a business

look.title: Sort the Farm
look.text: A family farm in central Illinois grows corn. It has 500 acres of soil, a tractor, a grain bin, a farmer and two hired workers. The farmer decided to borrow money and start selling sweet corn at a roadside stand.
look.prompt: Put each item into one of the four factors of production. Which item is the easiest to mix up?

check.q: A bakery's oven is which factor of production?
check.why: Capital is a tool or machine made by people to produce other goods. An oven fits.

check.q: Which is an example of land in economics?
choices: A river used to water crops
check.why: Land means natural resources. A river is natural; the building is capital and the driver is labor.

check.q: Why is money not counted as capital in economics?
choices: Money is a kind of land
Money cannot make anything by itself; it buys the tools that do
Money is always scarce and capital is not
check.why: Capital means the tools and machines themselves. Money is used to buy them but does not produce goods.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants and Choices
lessons.mainIdea: Economists treat needs and wants alike as choices, because even basic needs come in many forms with different costs.
reading: Most people say food is a need and a phone is a want. That is a helpful starting point. Everyone needs food, water, clothing and shelter to live. A *need* is something required to survive. A *want* is something we would like to have but can live without.

Economists add a twist. You need food, but you do not need steak. A bag of rice at $4 and a steak dinner at $40 both meet the need for food. (Prices are examples.) The extra $36 is a choice. So economists look less at the label and more at the trade-off. Each way of meeting a need has a different cost.

This matters for scarcity. Needs are limited, but the ways of meeting them are not. People always want a little better food, a little nicer home. That is why wants keep growing even when needs are met. Families must still decide how much of their money goes to each.

words.d: something a person must have to survive, such as food, water, clothing and shelter
something a person would like to have but can live without

look.title: Three Ways to Eat Dinner
look.cite: Made-up example prices for this lesson
look.prompt: All four meet the need for dinner. How much more does the restaurant cost than rice and beans? What does the extra money buy?

check.q: Which item is a need?
check.why: Water is required to survive. The others are wants.

check.q: Rice costs $4 and a steak dinner costs $40 (example prices). How much extra is spent on the want part of the steak dinner?
check.why: Both meet the need for food. $40 minus $4 is $36 spent beyond the basic need.

check.q: Why do economists say needs can still involve choices?
choices: Needs can be met in many ways, and each costs something different
The government pays for all needs
check.why: Food, clothing and shelter come in many forms at many prices, so people still choose.

sections.title: The Real Cost of a Choice

lessons.title: Opportunity Cost
lessons.mainIdea: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next-best thing you give up.
reading: Go back to Maya. She can take the garden job or go to summer school. If she picks summer school, she gives up $1,920 in wages. That lost pay is part of the cost. Economists call it the *opportunity cost*: the value of the next-best choice you gave up.

Here is how to find it. First, list the real choices. Second, rank them. Third, the opportunity cost is only the one right behind your top choice. Suppose Maya's options are summer school, the job, or sleeping in. If the job is her second choice, the opportunity cost of school is the job, not the job plus sleeping in. She could never have done all three.

A common mistake is to add up everything you gave up. Opportunity cost is not a list. It is the single next-best option. Another mistake is to count only money. Maya's job also offers time outdoors and a reference for later. Those count too.
*Trade-offs* are all the options you give up. The opportunity cost is the best one of those. Every choice has one, even a free concert. The concert is free, but the two hours are not.

words.d: the value of the next-best choice you give up when you make a decision
giving up some of one thing to get more of another; all the options not chosen

look.title: Three Ways to Spend Saturday
look.text: Luis ranks his Saturday choices: 1) a paid babysitting job for $40 (example pay), 2) a basketball tournament with friends, 3) a free museum day. He chooses babysitting.
look.prompt: What is Luis's opportunity cost? Why is it not the tournament plus the museum?

check.q: Luis ranks babysitting first, the tournament second and the museum third. He babysits. What is his opportunity cost?
check.why: Opportunity cost is only the next-best option, which is the tournament.

check.q: A free outdoor concert lasts 3 hours. Why does it still have an opportunity cost?
choices: The 3 hours could have been used for something else
check.why: Time is scarce. The next-best use of those 3 hours is the opportunity cost.

check.q: Maya would earn $1,920 at a job (example). Summer school charges $150. What is the full cost of summer school to Maya?
check.why: The full cost is the money paid plus the wages given up: $150 + $1,920 = $2,070.

lessons.title: Thinking at the Margin
lessons.mainIdea: Most choices are about one more or one less, so compare the extra benefit with the extra cost.
reading: You are at a pizza party. The first slice tastes amazing. The second is still good. By the fourth slice you feel a bit sick. Each extra slice gives you less joy than the one before. The extra joy from one more slice is its *marginal* benefit. Marginal means one more unit.

Now try it with studying. Suppose a test is tomorrow. As an example, the first hour of study raises your score by 10 points. The second hour adds 6 points. The third hour adds 2 points. The fourth hour adds 0, because you are tired. The *marginal benefit* of each hour keeps falling.

The *marginal cost* is what one more hour costs you. Say each hour costs you an hour of sleep or play. Is the third hour worth 2 points? Maybe. Is the fourth hour worth 0 points? No. A smart rule: keep going while the marginal benefit is bigger than the marginal cost. Stop when it is not.

People rarely choose all or nothing. They choose a little more or a little less. That is why economists say to think at the margin, not in totals. The total benefit of 4 hours is 18 points, but the fourth hour alone added nothing.

words.d: one more or one less unit; the next step in a choice
the extra benefit from doing or having one more unit of something
the extra cost of doing or making one more unit of something

look.title: Points Gained per Study Hour
look.prompt: What is the total gain after 3 hours? If one hour of rest is worth 3 points to you, how many hours should you study?

check.q: Using the study table, what is the total score gain after 3 hours?
What does 'marginal' mean in economics?
choices: One more or one less unit
check.why: Marginal thinking looks at the next unit, not the total.

check.q: The fifth slice of pizza gives you a stomachache. What is true about its marginal benefit?
choices: It is the highest of all slices
It is low or even negative
It cannot be measured at all
check.why: Marginal benefit usually falls with each extra unit, and it can drop below zero.

lessons.title: Weighing Costs and Benefits
lessons.mainIdea: Cost-benefit analysis lists the costs and benefits of each option, puts numbers on them where you can, and compares.
reading: Maya's family used a *decision grid*. Choices go across the top. The things that matter go down the side. Then each box gets a score. It turns a messy feeling into something you can see.

Here is a worked example. Scores run from 1 (poor) to 5 (great). Money: job 5, school 1. Learning: job 2, school 5. Time with friends: job 3, school 3. Ready for high school: job 2, school 5. Add them up. The job gets 5 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 12. School gets 1 + 5 + 3 + 5 = 14. School wins by 2 points.

But the family says money matters twice as much right now. So they double the money row. The job now gets 17 and school gets 15. The winner flipped. That shows the key idea of *cost-benefit analysis*: the answer depends on what you value most. The grid does not decide for you. It shows your reasons clearly.

A common mistake is to leave out hidden costs, like lost wages or travel time. Another is to count a cost you cannot get back. If Maya already paid a $20 fee that no refund will return, it should not change her choice now.

words.d: a way of deciding by listing and comparing the costs and benefits of each option
a table with choices across the top and criteria down the side, scored to compare options

look.title: Your Own Grid
look.text: A sixth grader can join the robotics club or the soccer team. Both meet after school on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Robotics costs $50 for parts (example). Soccer costs $80 for fees and cleats (example).
look.prompt: Make a decision grid with 4 criteria. Score each from 1 to 5. Which wins? Would doubling one row change the result?

check.q: In a decision grid, the job scores 5, 2, 3 and 2. What is its total?
The money row is doubled. The job's money score was 5. By how much does the job's total rise?
check.why: Doubling 5 gives 10, which adds 5 more points to the total.

check.q: Maya already paid a $20 fee she cannot get back. How should it affect her choice now?
choices: It should make her pick school
It should not change her choice, since it is gone either way
She should add $40 to the school side
It doubles the cost of the job
check.why: Money spent that cannot be recovered is the same no matter what she picks, so it should not sway the decision.

lessons.title: How Incentives Change Choices
lessons.mainIdea: Incentives are rewards and costs that push people toward or away from a choice.
reading: A store puts up a sign: "Buy one, get one free." More people buy. A city raises the fine for parking in a bus lane from $50 to $250 (example amounts). Fewer people park there. Both are *incentives*. An incentive is anything that changes the benefits or costs of a choice.

A *positive incentive* is a reward that encourages an action. Extra recess for finished work, a bonus for a salesperson, and a lower price are examples. A *negative incentive* is a cost or punishment that discourages an action. Late fees, fines and higher prices are examples.

Economists expect people to respond to incentives in fairly predictable ways. When the reward for something goes up, people do more of it. When the cost goes up, people do less of it. This does not mean people only care about money. Praise, grades, time and safety are incentives too.

Adam Smith wrote about this in 1776. He saw that bakers and butchers work hard because it pays them to. Their self-interest leads them to serve customers well. A baker who sells stale bread loses customers, so the baker has a reason to bake good bread.

words.d: a reward or cost that encourages or discourages a certain choice
a reward that encourages people to do something
a cost or penalty that discourages people from doing something

look.title: The Butcher, the Brewer and the Baker
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 2, 1776
look.prompt: "Benevolence" means kindness. What incentive does Smith say makes the baker bake bread for you?

check.q: A library ends late fees. Which kind of incentive was removed?
check.why: A late fee is a penalty that discourages returning books late, so it is a negative incentive.

check.q: A city raises a parking fine from $50 to $250 (example). What do economists predict?
check.why: Raising the cost of an action gives people a reason to do less of it.

check.q: Which is a positive incentive?
choices: A $20 bonus for each new customer
check.why: A bonus is a reward that encourages the action.

lessons.title: When Incentives Surprise Us
lessons.mainIdea: Incentives can lead to results nobody planned, so good rules think about how people will really respond.
reading: A teacher offers one prize point for every book a student reads. Soon students pick the thinnest books they can find. The teacher wanted more reading, but the incentive rewarded the number of books, not the pages or the learning. This is an *unintended consequence*: a result nobody planned.

Here is a worked example. Before the prize, a class reads 20 books a month, about 200 pages each. That is 4,000 pages. After the prize, the class reads 40 books, but they average 50 pages. That is 2,000 pages. The book count doubled, but pages read fell by half.

Good rule-makers ask, "How will people really react?" The teacher could reward pages or minutes instead. Cities, schools and businesses all face this question. A tax, a fine, a price or a prize will change what people do, sometimes in ways the designers did not expect.

words.d: a result of a rule or choice that was not planned or expected
a reward or cost that encourages or discourages a certain choice

look.title: The Cleanup Contest
look.text: A town pays $1 (example) for every bag of trash people bring from the park. Within a month, some people are bringing trash from home in extra bags to collect the money.
look.prompt: What did the town want? What did the incentive really reward? How could the town change the rule?

check.q: A class read 20 books of 200 pages before a prize and 40 books of 50 pages after. How did total pages change?
check.why: 20 x 200 = 4,000 pages before; 40 x 50 = 2,000 after. Pages fell by half.

check.q: What is an unintended consequence?
check.why: An unintended consequence is an outcome the rule-makers did not expect.

check.q: The trash contest pays per bag. Which rule change best fixes the problem?
choices: Pay only for trash from home
Pay for the weight of trash picked up in the park, checked on site
check.why: Rewarding park trash checked on site ties the reward to the goal the town wanted.

lessons.title: Families, Schools and Towns Choose
lessons.mainIdea: Groups face scarcity too: a family, a school or a town must give up one use of its money to fund another.
reading: A school has $10,000 to spend this year (example). The science teachers want new microscopes for $6,000. The coaches want new uniforms for $5,000. The library wants books for $4,000. Together that is $15,000. The school must give up $5,000 of the wish list.

If the school buys microscopes and books, it spends $10,000. The opportunity cost is the uniforms. If it buys uniforms and books, it spends $9,000. The opportunity cost is the microscopes. Either way, something is left out. That is scarcity for a group.

Towns face the same problem. A town can fix roads or build a new park with its budget. States choose between schools, highways and health care. Groups often use votes, meetings or budgets to decide. The economic question is the same one Maya asked: what are we giving up?

words.d: a plan for how to spend and save a set amount of money
the value of the next-best choice you give up when you make a decision

look.title: A School's Wish List
look.prompt: Which two items fit inside $10,000? Which pair costs the least, and how much is left over?

check.q: Microscopes cost $6,000 and books cost $4,000 (example). The budget is $10,000. How much is left after buying both?
The school buys uniforms and books. What is the opportunity cost?
check.why: The item left out, the microscopes, is what the school gave up.

check.q: Why does a whole town face scarcity?
choices: Towns have no money at all
Its money and land are limited, but people want many things
check.why: Groups have limited resources and many wants, just like people.

lessons.title: Choosing Like an Economist
lessons.mainIdea: Good choices come from naming the options, finding the opportunity cost, thinking at the margin and checking the incentives.
reading: You now have four tools. Scarcity says you must choose. Opportunity cost says every choice gives up the next-best option. Marginal thinking says to weigh one more step at a time. Incentives explain why people act as they do.

Here is Maya's final choice. She finds a middle path. She takes the job for 12 hours a week instead of 20 and signs up for a free online algebra course in the mornings. Her pay is 12 x $12 = $144 a week. Over 8 weeks that is $1,152. Compared with the full job, she gives up 8 hours a week, or $768 over the summer, to gain learning time.

That is thinking at the margin. She did not choose all job or all school. She asked whether the last 8 hours of work were worth more than 8 hours of algebra. For her, they were not. Another student might choose differently, and that is fine. Economics does not tell you what to value. It helps you see the trade-offs clearly.

words.d: giving up some of one thing to get more of another; all the options not chosen
the extra cost of doing or making one more unit of something

look.title: Check Maya's Math
look.text: Full job: 20 hours a week at $12 for 8 weeks. Part-time job: 12 hours a week at $12 for 8 weeks. All pay figures are examples.
look.prompt: Find the pay for each plan. What is the dollar difference? What does Maya get in return?

check.q: Maya works 12 hours a week at $12 an hour (example) for 8 weeks. What does she earn?
By choosing 12 hours instead of 20, how much pay does Maya give up over 8 weeks?
check.why: 8 fewer hours x $12 = $96 a week; $96 x 8 = $768.

check.q: Which question shows thinking at the margin?
choices: Are 8 more hours of work worth more than 8 hours of study?
What is the total of every job in town?
What did I buy last year?
check.why: Marginal thinking compares the benefit and cost of one more step.

review.q: Which is the best definition of opportunity cost?
choices: The next-best choice you gave up
review.why: Opportunity cost is only the single next-best option, not a list.

review.q: A tractor on an Illinois farm is which factor of production?
review.why: A tractor is a machine made to produce other goods, so it is capital.

review.q: A store offers a $5 coupon on shoes. What kind of incentive is this?
review.why: The coupon is a reward that encourages buying.

review.q: Study hours add 10, 6, 2 and 0 points (example). Which hour has the lowest marginal benefit?
review.why: Hour 4 adds 0 points, the smallest extra benefit.

review.q: Why does scarcity affect even very rich people?
choices: Time and other resources are still limited
review.why: Everyone has limited time and resources compared with their wants.

review.q: A town gives $1 per bag of trash and people bring trash from home. This is an example of what?
review.why: The incentive caused a result the town did not plan.

review.q: A job pays $10 an hour for 30 hours (example). Instead you go to a free camp for those 30 hours. What is the money part of the camp's opportunity cost?
review.why: The camp is free, but you give up 30 x $10 = $300 in wages.

review.q: A family doubles the money row in its decision grid, and a different option wins. What does this show?
choices: The best choice depends on what you value most
Money is the only thing that matters
review.why: Changing the weight of a value can change the result, so the answer depends on priorities.
